summary: This unit teaches you to give quality service to every client of a salon or spa: welcome her, find out what she needs, communicate clearly, keep her safe and comfortable, treat everyone fairly, handle complaints, collect and use feedback, and build loyalty. You will also learn the professional and ethical habits that make clients trust you.

blocks.p: This unit is about the part of your job that clients notice first and remember longest: how you make them feel. A client may forget the exact shade of her colour, but she will remember whether she was greeted warmly, listened to, kept safe and treated fairly. It is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees, and it applies to every service you will ever give: hair, nails, skin, make-up and body treatments.

Good service is not only about being nice. It is a set of skills you can learn and practise: communicating clearly, asking the right questions, working safely, keeping information private, solving problems and learning from what clients tell you. Salons and spas in Jamaica depend on regular clients and on word of mouth, so these skills are as important to the business as technical skill.

Welcome

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and two group practical tasks: handling client complaints in role plays and completing complaint records, and designing and running a client feedback survey with an improvement plan. The assessor looks at what you say and do, and at the records you keep, not only at the result.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In group practical work, photograph people from behind or at the side, or photograph only hands and papers. Never photograph a person's face unless she agrees and the Centre allows it. Use made-up names and details in role plays.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Client (customer) service** is everything the salon and its staff do to meet a client's needs and make her feel valued, from the first phone call to the follow-up after her visit. **Quality** service means doing this well every time, for every client, not only when you feel like it or when the owner is watching.

head: Type
Who they are
Examples
rows: External customers
People from outside the business who pay for its services and products.
A regular client; a walk-in; a hotel guest booking a massage; a parent bringing a child for a haircut.
Internal customers
People inside the business who depend on your help or your work to do their own job.
The stylist who needs you to shampoo her client on time; the receptionist who needs your free times; the next shift who need the station left clean.
Suppliers and visitors
People who deal with the business but do not have services.
A delivery driver; a product representative. Treat them politely too.

blocks.p: A **walk-in** is a client who comes in without an appointment. A **regular** is a client who comes back often. Both deserve respect, but you must be honest with a walk-in about how long she will wait.

head: Clients expect
What you do to deliver it
rows: A clean, safe place
Keep work areas tidy, tools disinfected and floors dry; use fresh towels.
A polite, friendly welcome
Greet her within moments, smile, use her name.
Skill and care
Do the service properly; work only within your training; ask for help when needed.
To be listened to
Ask, listen, repeat back, and agree what will be done before you start.
Honest advice and a fair price
Say what is possible, how long it takes and what it costs. No false promises.
Privacy and respect
Keep her information private; cover her properly; ask before touching.
Good use of her time
Start on time; tell her if there is a delay; do not rush her either.

blocks.p: A client forms an opinion of you and of the salon in the **first few seconds**. She notices how you look, whether you smile and look at her, how the reception area looks and smells, and how long she waits before someone speaks to her. A first impression is hard to change, so get it right.

ul: **Look:** clean uniform or neat clothes, tidy hair, clean short nails, closed shoes suited to the work, and little jewellery that could scratch or catch.

**Hygiene:** wash your hands, bathe daily, keep your breath fresh and use a deodorant. Use only a light perfume or none at all, because strong scent can upset clients with allergies, asthma or headaches.
**Posture:** stand or sit upright, face the client, keep your arms relaxed and not folded.
**Place:** a clean reception, fresh smell, tidy magazines, a price list in view and no rubbish or dirty towels in sight.
**Phone:** keep your personal phone out of sight while you work with a client.

head: Quality
What it looks like in the salon
rows: Politeness and a positive attitude
Please, thank you, a smile, and a helpful answer even when you are busy.
Patience
Explaining again to a nervous client; not rushing an older client.
Honesty and reliability
Saying 'I am not trained for that'; doing what you promised.
Punctuality
Arriving on time, starting on time and keeping to the booking times, so clients are seen on time and co-workers are not left to cover for you.
Calm under pressure
Staying professional when the salon is crowded or a client is difficult.
Willingness to learn
Accepting feedback, practising, asking questions.

blocks.note: Leave your own problems at the door. A client has come for a pleasant experience, not to hear about your bad day. If you are upset, take a short break, breathe, and then return to work polite and calm. Do not take it out on clients or co-workers.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Service standards** are the salon's own rules for how every client is looked after, so that service is the same whoever is on duty. For example: greet every client within one minute; tell any client who waits more than ten minutes how long it will be; offer a drink to every waiting client; answer the phone within a few rings; clean the station after every client. The figures are set by each salon, so follow your salon's own standards.

ul: **For the client:** she gets the result she wanted, feels safe and respected, and enjoys her time.
**For staff:** happy clients are easier to work with, ask for you by name, and may tip. The job is more satisfying.

**For the business:** most of a salon's income comes from regular clients. It costs far less to keep a client than to find a new one. A satisfied client tells friends and family: this free advertising is called **word of mouth**. An unhappy client tells even more people, and today she can tell hundreds online in minutes.

blocks.note: In a small Jamaican community, everyone knows everyone. One careless remark or a badly handled complaint can reach the whole district by the weekend. Good service protects the salon's name.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Communication is how you find out what a client needs and how you let her know what will happen. It has three parts: what you say, how you say it, and what your body says.

head: Part
What it is
Good practice
rows: Words (verbal)
The words you choose.
Plain, clear words the client understands
Polite phrases: please, thank you, excuse me
No slang that could offend; no trade words she does not know
Tone of voice
How your voice sounds: warm, cold, bored or angry. It shows your feelings.
Warm and calm
Not too loud or too soft
The same helpful tone when you are tired or busy
Body language (non-verbal)
Your face, eyes, posture and gestures.
Smile and eye contact
Face the client; lean in a little when she speaks
Avoid folded arms, frowning, sighing and looking at the clock

blocks.note: If your words and your body language disagree, the client believes your body. Saying 'No problem' while rolling your eyes tells her it is a problem.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Trade words such as 'desquamation', 'comedones' or 'porosity' mean nothing to most clients and can make her feel small or confused. Say 'dead skin cells', 'blackheads' and 'how well your hair takes in water'. If you must use a trade word, explain it in plain English straight away. In Jamaica, many clients are most comfortable in Patois. You may answer in the way she speaks, politely, and you must never mock anyone's way of speaking. Keep notices and written information in clear English.
Listening is not just waiting for your turn to talk. **Active listening** means giving the client your full attention so that you understand what she means, not only what she says.

flow: Stop what you are doing and face her
Look at her and keep your body language open
Let her finish without interrupting
Nod or say 'I see' now and then
Repeat the main points back in your own words
Ask a question if anything is not clear
Confirm what you will do

blocks.p: Example of repeating back: 'So you would like to keep the length but take off the dry ends, and you want it easy to style for work. Is that right?' This lets her correct you before you start, which saves mistakes and complaints.

head: Type
What it is
Examples
When to use it
rows: Open question
Needs more than yes or no; the client answers in her own words. Often starts with what, how, why, tell me about.
What would you like done today?
How do you look after your nails at home?
Tell me about the last time you used this product.
At the start of a consultation, to learn her wishes, habits and worries.
Closed question
Can be answered with yes or no, or one word.
Is the water comfortable?
Have you had a skin test for this colour?
Do you have any allergies?
To check facts, safety and comfort quickly during the service.

blocks.p: A good consultation uses both. Open questions give you the picture; closed questions confirm the details.

ul: **Rapport** is a friendly, trusting relationship between you and the client. Build it with a smile, using her name, remembering something she told you last time and showing real interest.

**Empathy** means understanding and sharing how another person feels. It is different from simply feeling sorry for her. When a client says she is nervous about her first wax, empathy sounds like: 'It is normal to feel nervous the first time. I will tell you what I am doing at each step, and you can tell me to stop.'

**Small talk** should be friendly and light: the weather, her plans for the weekend, hair and skin care tips. Avoid politics, religion, gossip about other clients, personal questions about money or relationships, and complaints about your job or the salon.

head: Situation
What to do
rows: Answering the phone
Answer within a few rings, smile (it changes your voice), say the salon's name, a greeting and your name
Speak clearly and a little slower than normal
Do not eat or chew while talking
Taking a booking
Write down her name, number, service, day and time
Repeat the details back to check them
Tell her about the late-arrival policy and the price if she asks
Taking a message
Write who called, the number, the message, the date and time and your name
Pass it on the same day
Phone calls while you are with a client
The client in front of you comes first; let the receptionist or voicemail answer
Never take a personal call
Chat apps and social media (many Jamaican salons book on WhatsApp)
Reply politely and soon, with correct, up-to-date prices and times
Never share one client's details with another
Do not discuss a complaint in a public comment: invite her to message or call privately

blocks.h: Things that get in the way of communication

head: Barrier
What you can do
rows: Noise from dryers, music and the street
Lower the music; move to a quieter spot for the consultation.
Trade words and jargon
Use plain words.
Assuming you know what she wants
Ask and check back.
A client who is hard of hearing
Face her, speak clearly and a little slower, not louder; use a notepad or pictures; make sure she can see your lips.
A client who speaks little English (for example, a tourist)
Speak simply; use pictures and a colour chart; write numbers; ask a colleague who speaks her language.
Your own mood or tiredness
Take a breath and focus on her.

ul: Use the appointment book or system to book the right service with the right person for the right amount of time. A relaxer takes far longer than a trim, so give each service enough time.
Take her full name and phone number, and confirm the service, day and time by repeating them back.
Say the price (or the price range) and anything she must do before she comes, for example 'come with your hair unwashed' or 'come for a skin test two days before the colour'.
Send or give a reminder the day before, if the client agreed.

A **late-arrival and cancellation policy**, explained when the booking is made, helps everyone. It must be fair: allow for real emergencies and apply it the same way to all clients, with the supervisor deciding exceptions.

flow: Stop and look up when she comes in
Smile and greet her, using her name if you know it
Check her booking, or ask what she needs if she is a walk-in
Offer her a seat and a drink of water
Tell her honestly how long she will wait
Tell the stylist or therapist that she has arrived
Take her to the work area when it is ready

ul: **Walk-ins:** do not promise what you cannot do. Say honestly when the next space is, and let her choose to wait, return later or book. Never push a booked client aside to fit her in.

**Waiting clients:** tell them if there is a delay and how long it will be, apologise, and give a drink or a magazine. A client who knows how long she must wait is far happier than one who is left wondering.
**Extra care for some clients:** an older client may need an arm to the chair, a mother with small children may need a safe corner, and a client in pain or tired may need a quiet seat.
Start on time and keep to the booking time. If you are running late, tell the next client early, apologise and offer a drink or a later time.

Be friendly but keep the service moving. If a client wants to chat for a long time while others wait, stay warm and say something like 'I would love to hear more, but I need to keep to the time for the next client.'
Do not rush the client either. A quick service done badly leads to a complaint and a re-do, which costs more time.

blocks.p: A consultation is a short, private conversation before the service, in which you find out what the client wants, check that the service is safe for her, and agree the plan.

flow: Welcome her and seat her comfortably
Read her record card
Ask open questions about what she wants
Look at (and, where suitable, feel) her hair, skin or nails
Check for contra-indications and skin tests
Explain what you suggest, the time and the price
Agree the plan and get her consent
Write it on her record

head: Find out
Why
rows: What she wants and why (a wedding, a job interview, a new look)
So the result fits her purpose and timing.
Photos she likes
A picture removes guesswork. Check what is realistic for her hair or skin.
Her past services and any reactions
Past chemical services, reactions and allergies decide what is safe today.
Health, medicines, pregnancy, allergies, sensitive skin
Some conditions or medicines make a service unsafe or change the result.
Her budget and time
So the plan is realistic.

blocks.note: A contra-indication is a reason not to give a service, or to change it, such as an infection, an open cut, a rash, a sunburn or an allergy. If you find one, explain kindly and privately, offer a safe alternative where possible, and refer her to a doctor if needed. Many products need a skin (patch) test first, often 24 to 48 hours before the service: follow the manufacturer's instructions. A client's safety always matters more than a sale.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Say what is possible and what is not, and why. A very dark hair colour cannot be lightened to platinum safely in one visit; a short cut cannot be made long again the same day.
Never promise results you cannot be sure of ('no more spots', 'your hair will grow 10 cm'). Say 'this should help' or 'most clients see an improvement', and explain what she must do at home.
If you cannot do what she asks safely or well, say so politely and offer another choice.
Give the price and time before you start. A surprise bill is one of the most common causes of complaints.
Repeat the plan back and get her agreement before you start.

blocks.p: 'Going the extra mile' means doing a small thing beyond what was asked that makes a client feel special, without cost to the salon or breaking any rule. Examples: offering an umbrella or calling a taxi for an older client when it rains; remembering that a client takes her tea without sugar; helping a client with a heavy shopping bag; sending a short birthday message to clients who agreed to be contacted; showing a nervous first-time client around before her service.

blocks.note: Going the extra mile never means giving away free products or services without the manager's permission, or breaking a safety rule to please a client.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Keeping clients safe and respected: ethics and privacy

blocks.p: Clients trust you with their hair, skin and body, and with personal information. Professional **ethics** are the standards of right and wrong behaviour that guide you at work, even when nobody is watching.

blocks.h: Comfort, privacy and dignity during a service

ul: Check comfort often: 'Is the water comfortable?', 'Is the pressure all right?', 'Is the chair at the right height?' Stop at once if she feels pain, burning or dizziness.
Test the heat of water, wax or tools on the inside of your own wrist before they touch the client.
Protect her clothes with a gown and cape, and her dignity with towels: for body treatments, keep her covered except for the area being worked on.
Ask before you touch her face, head or body, and explain what you will do.
Close the door or screen for private treatments. Knock and wait before entering a room where a client is undressed.
Show that you are clean: wash your hands where she can see you; use fresh towels and clean, disinfected tools and single-use items once only.

head: Principle
In practice
Not like this
rows: Honesty
Correct prices, true statements about products and results.
Saying a product will 'cure' a problem; charging more than the price list.
Working within your training
Telling a client 'I am not trained for that; my colleague is' or booking another time.
Trying a service you have not learnt 'because she will not know'.
Putting safety first
Checking contra-indications, doing skin tests, referring to a doctor even if it loses a sale.
Skipping the test because the salon is busy.
Confidentiality
Keeping a client's details and what she tells you private.
Gossiping about her hair loss, health or personal life.
Fairness
Treating all clients equally and serving walk-ins and bookings fairly.
Serving friends first or turning away clients you do not like.
Respect for colleagues
Not talking badly about co-workers or competitors in front of clients.
Arguing in the salon; criticising another stylist's work to a client.
Honest selling
Recommending what suits her and explaining why; accepting 'no'.
Pushing the dearest product to earn commission.

blocks.p: **Confidentiality** means keeping a client's personal details private. This covers her name, phone number, address, health information, allergies, the services she has had, what she spends and what she says about her private life.

ul: Keep record cards in a locked drawer or a password-protected system; let only the staff who need them see them.
Do not leave cards, the appointment book or a phone screen where others can read them.
Do not discuss a client with other clients, or with friends outside the salon.
Get permission before photographing a client or posting her picture, name or story on social media, and write down that she agreed.
Do not give a client's phone number to anyone else, including a friend who 'only wants to say hello'.

blocks.note: Jamaica's Data Protection Act is about how personal information is collected, used and protected: only collect what you need, use it for the purpose the client agreed to, keep it accurate and secure, and do not share it without a good reason. Follow your salon's own privacy rules and ask your supervisor if you are unsure.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Follow the salon's policy on tips and gifts. Accept thanks politely. Never ask for tips, never give a client a favour that breaks salon rules (such as cutting her price without permission), and report any gift that seems intended to get special treatment.

Jamaican salons and spas serve people of every age, skin and hair type, religion, culture, size, income and ability, as well as visitors from other countries. **Discrimination** means treating someone unfairly because of who she is. It is wrong, it hurts clients, it damages the salon's name, and it may be against the law. Fair service means every client gets the same care, honesty and respect.

ul: Never joke about, comment on or stare at a client's body, background, accent, age or belief.
Do not assume. Ask: 'How do you usually wear your hair for your faith or culture?'
Learn to work with all hair and skin types. If you do not know, ask your instructor or supervisor before the service.
Treat a client without much money with the same politeness as a wealthy one.

head: Client
How you adapt
rows: Wheelchair user
Ask what help she wants; do not push the chair without asking
Keep the way clear; check the treatment room is reachable and the basin or couch suits her
Speak to her, not only to her companion
Hard of hearing
Face her and speak clearly; use notes or pictures
Reduce background noise
Visually impaired
Tell her who you are and what you are doing before you do it
Describe the room and products; guide with your arm if she asks
Older client
Allow extra time; offer an arm; use a comfortable chair
Check she is not dizzy when sitting up from a basin
Child
Talk to the child and the parent; a parent stays nearby
Use a cushion or booster seat; keep tools out of reach
Pregnant client
Ask about comfort, and about products or treatments that are unsuitable in pregnancy
Follow the product maker's instructions and refer if unsure
Nervous or first-time client
Explain each step before you start
Check comfort often; let her know she can say stop
Client from another country who speaks little English
Speak simply and slowly; use pictures, a colour chart and written numbers
Ask a colleague who speaks her language to help
Client with religious or cultural requirements
Ask what she needs: for example, a client who follows the Rastafari faith may want her locs handled in a certain way; a Muslim client may want a private area and a female stylist
Remember that some clients, such as many Seventh-day Adventists, keep Saturday as a day of worship and will not book then

blocks.p: Clients judge the whole salon, not only the person who served her. Teamwork means staff help each other so that every client gets a smooth, on-time service. Your **internal customers** are the colleagues who depend on you.

head: Who
How teamwork helps the client
rows: Receptionist
Books the right time, passes on messages, tells the stylist when the client arrives, so the stylist is ready on time.
Junior or assistant
Shampoos and prepares clients properly and quickly, so the stylist can keep to her bookings.
Free colleague
Greets a waiting client, offers a drink and explains a delay when a co-worker is running late.
Everyone
Keeps stock rooms tidy, reports low stock, cleans stations after use, and shares important client information such as allergies.

ul: **Hand-over:** if a colleague must leave in the middle of a service, the supervisor agrees who takes over, and the colleague gives clear information on what has been done and what is planned. Tell the client what is happening, so she is not surprised.
**Communication:** speak politely to colleagues, say please and thank you, and pass on messages.
**Disagreements:** never argue in front of clients. Move away, calm down and discuss it privately, or ask the supervisor to help.

**Covering for each other:** the salon works best when each person does her own share and offers help when she is free. Do not blame others when something goes wrong; fix the problem first and discuss the cause afterwards.

blocks.p: Every salon gets complaints sometimes. A client who complains is giving you a chance to put things right and to keep her. Many more unhappy clients say nothing and simply do not return. A complaint also shows you what to improve. How you handle it often matters more to the client than the mistake itself.

head: Common causes
Examples
rows: The result
Colour not as expected; a cut uneven; a style that did not last.
The service
A long wait; being rushed; a rough pair of hands; poor hygiene.
People
A rude remark; being ignored; gossip.
Money
A price different from the one quoted; a wrong bill.
Safety
A burn, a reaction, a sore scalp after a style.

flow: Stay calm and move her to a quiet area
Listen to the whole complaint without interrupting
Apologise that she is unhappy, without arguing or blaming
Ask questions and check the facts, including looking at the problem and the record
Offer a fair solution within your authority, or call the supervisor
Act on it as promised and thank her
Record the complaint and what was done
Follow up later to check that she is happy

head: Step
Reason
rows: Move to a quiet area
She can speak freely; other clients are not upset; you both stay calmer.
Listen without interrupting
She feels heard, and her anger drops. You may learn the real problem, which is not always the first thing she says.
Apologise
You are sorry that she is unhappy. You do not have to agree that it was your fault before you check the facts.
Check the facts
Look at the hair, skin or nails in good light. Check the record: the product, timing and what was agreed.
Offer a solution
Clients want the problem fixed. Giving a choice gives her some control.
Record and follow up
Shows she matters, and helps the manager to spot patterns.

head: Say
Do not say
rows: 'I am sorry that you are not happy. Let me look at it.'
'That never happens here.' (It tells her she is lying.)
'Thank you for telling me.'
'You should have said something at the time.' (It blames her.)
'Here is what I can do.'
'There is nothing I can do.'
'I will ask my supervisor to help you with that.'
'That's not my job.' or 'It was the other stylist.'

blocks.h: What you may decide, and what goes to the supervisor

head: You can usually decide
The supervisor or manager decides
rows: Apologising and listening
Refunds and free services
Looking at the problem and checking the record
Compensation, or anything that costs the salon money
Re-doing or adjusting a small part of your own work, if the supervisor's rules allow it
Anything that involves an injury, a reaction, a threat or the police
Explaining what was done and why
A client who is still unhappy after your solution

blocks.p: Your salon's rules set the exact limits. If a complaint is more than you are allowed or able to solve, call the supervisor politely and stay with the client until she arrives. Briefly tell the supervisor the facts so the client does not have to repeat everything.

ul: Stay calm. Lower your voice and speak slowly. Do not argue, shout or swear back.
Do not take it personally. She is angry about the problem.
Keep a safe distance and never touch her.
Call the supervisor at once. If she threatens you or others, the supervisor decides whether to ask her to leave or call the police.
Write down what happened afterwards.

blocks.p: If a client says that a product burns or her skin is reacting, stop the service at once, remove the product (for example, rinse it off with cool or lukewarm running water as the product instructions say), check her skin, and call the supervisor. Give first aid, advise her to see a doctor if the skin is red, sore or blistered, and write it in the accident book. Safety first; discuss the complaint afterwards.

**Service recovery** means the steps a business takes to put things right and win back a client after a mistake. A gesture can help, always with the manager's agreement: a free re-do, a small discount on the next visit or a free treatment. Offer it sincerely, not as a way to stop her talking. Clients who see a problem solved well often become more loyal than before.

head: Record
Example
rows: Date and time
Client's name and contact
Made-up name and number for training
What the complaint was, in her own words
'My scalp is sore and I have headaches since the braids.'
What you found
Redness at the front hairline; braids tight.
What was agreed, and who agreed it
Loosen the front braids today at no charge; supervisor agreed.
Who handled it
Name of the staff member and the supervisor.
Follow-up
Call on Friday, if the client agrees.
Possible cause and change
Braids too tight at the front: check tension and advise the client.

blocks.p: Complaints written down and looked at together show patterns, such as long waits on Saturdays or one product causing reactions. The manager can then fix the cause, not only the single complaint.

blocks.h: Complaints on social media and review sites

ul: A public complaint is still a complaint. A supervisor should agree the reply.
Reply politely and soon, thank her for the feedback, apologise that her experience was poor and invite her to contact the salon privately to put it right.
Never argue online, name the client or reveal details of her service. Never ask friends to post false good reviews.
Use the lesson to improve.

blocks.p: You cannot fix what you do not know about. Feedback tells the salon what clients like, what annoys them and what to change. **Client satisfaction** means how pleased a client is that the service met her needs. Because many unhappy clients do not complain, you must ask.

head: Way to collect feedback
Good points
Take care
rows: Asking in person at the end of the visit
Quick and friendly.
Clients may be too polite to be honest, especially with the stylist in front of her.
Comment card or short survey, with a box
Can be anonymous, so more honest.
Keep it short; read the cards.
Text, chat message or online survey after the visit
Reaches clients at home.
Only for clients who agreed to be contacted.
Reading reviews and social media comments
Shows what the public thinks.
Reply politely; remember reviews are one person's view.
A follow-up call a few days after a new chemical service
Catches problems early and shows care.
Only if she agreed; keep it short and polite.

ul: Five to eight short questions in plain words: the welcome, waiting time, cleanliness, the service, advice, and value for money.
A **1 to 5 score** for each (1 is poor, 5 is excellent), with a space for one open question such as 'What one thing could we do better?'
No names, unless the client chooses to give one. Say clearly that it is anonymous and what it will be used for.
A box in a place where she can post it privately.

blocks.p: The **average** (mean) is the total of the scores divided by the number of scores. Example: six clients score 'waiting time' as 3, 2, 4, 3, 3 and 2. The total is 3 + 2 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 2 = 17. Divide by 6: 17 ÷ 6 = 2.83, which you may round to 2.8 out of 5.

head: Question
Scores from six clients
Total
Average
rows: Welcome
Waiting time
Cleanliness
Value for money

blocks.p: Here the lowest average is waiting time (2.8), so that is where the salon should act first. Work every average twice to be sure.

ul: Draw the vertical axis from 0 to 5 and mark it in equal steps; label it 'Average score'.
Write the questions along the bottom, one bar for each, all bars the same width with equal gaps.
Draw each bar to the height of its average; give the chart a title.
Use a ruler and keep the scale the same for every bar.

flow: Collect and read all the feedback, good and bad
Add up the scores and work out the averages
Look for comments that come up again and again
Pick the three lowest scores
Plan one change for each: what, who and by when
Share praise with the staff and the plan with the team
Collect feedback again and check that the change worked

head: Problem found
Action plan
rows: Waiting time scores lowest (2.8)
What: tell each client the expected wait on arrival and offer a drink. Who: the receptionist. By when: from Monday; check scores again in four weeks.
Clients say advice is rushed
What: give two minutes of aftercare advice at the end of every service. Who: all stylists. By when: from next week.

blocks.p: A good plan is specific, has a named person and a date, and is checked later. 'Try harder' is not a plan, and ignoring the lowest scores or removing the question from the card does not solve anything.
A **loyal** client keeps coming back and brings her friends. Loyalty is earned by good service every time, not by price alone.

head: Way to build loyalty
How
rows: A safe, good service every time
Keep standards the same whoever is on duty.
Use her name and remember her preferences
Note her favourite stylist, her drink, how she likes her nails or what she is allergic to, on the record card, so any staff member can give the same personal service.
Honest advice and clear aftercare
Tell her what suits her and how to keep the result. This is part of the service, not a sales trick.
Rebook before she leaves
'Shall I book your next retouch for four weeks from today?'
Reward regular clients
A loyalty card (stamped at each visit, with a reward after a set number of visits), a birthday treat, an offer for rebooking. Keep rewards fair and agreed by the manager.
Follow up and handle complaints well
A call a few days after a new service, if she agreed; quick, kind handling of any problem.
Ask for referrals
A small thank-you for a friend she brings.

blocks.p: Aftercare tells the client how to look after the result at home and avoid problems. Base it on what you found in the consultation, give the reason for each point and keep it short. Suggest products that suit her, explain how to use them, and never pressure her to buy. She decides.

blocks.note: A client's record card is also a loyalty tool. Noting 'prefers Odette, no scent in products, likes herbal tea' lets the next person make her feel known, but remember it is personal information: keep it private.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Practical tasks: complaints and the feedback survey

blocks.p: Both practical tasks are group tasks. Each member must show her own skills, so prepare so that you can speak and act with confidence.

ul: Each member handles one complaint as the staff member. The others play the client and the supervisor, and one keeps notes.
Use made-up names and details. Keep the role play calm: no shouting or touching, even when acting angry.

Show every step: move her to a quiet area, listen without interrupting, apologise, check the facts, offer a solution within your authority or call the supervisor, thank her and say what will happen next.
Fill in the complaint record form clearly and completely, with the date, the complaint, what you found, what was agreed and the follow-up.
As a group, write an action list: one change the salon could make for each complaint so that it does not happen again.
Photograph each stage from behind or the side, or show only hands and papers.

head: Complaint card
Likely solution to discuss
rows: Colour darker than wanted
Look at it in good light; check the colour record; offer a correction by a senior stylist; supervisor agrees on any charge.
A long wait
Apologise; explain the reason; offer a drink; supervisor may offer a gesture; the action list: tell clients waiting times.
Skin red after a facial
Check the skin; cool compress if appropriate; refer to a doctor if sore; accident record; supervisor.
Wrong price charged
Check the price list and the bill with the supervisor; correct it; apologise.
A rude remark
Listen; apologise; the supervisor speaks to the staff member; record.

ul: Design the card together: clear, polite questions in plain words, a 1 to 5 score and one open question.
Each member collects feedback from at least three people who agree, without writing their names. Do not interrupt a service or enter a treatment room during one.
Add up the scores for each question, work out the averages and double-check them. Draw an accurate bar chart.
Pick the three lowest scores and plan one improvement for each: what, who and by when.
Make an A3 poster with the card, the results, the chart and the plan. Each member presents one part and answers a question about it.
Do not argue with any answer: feedback is information, not an attack.

blocks.note: Use markers in a ventilated room and put the caps back on. Keep walkways clear while you work on the poster.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: I can explain what quality client service is, and say who external and internal customers are.
I can describe a good first impression and the personal qualities clients value.
I can explain service standards and why happy clients are important to the business.
I can use words, tone and body language to show I am listening and that I care.
I can ask open and closed questions and say when to use each.
I can show rapport and empathy, and choose safe topics for small talk.
I can handle telephone calls, bookings and messages politely.
I can welcome walk-in and waiting clients and manage my time.
I can carry out a consultation, check contra-indications and skin tests, and agree a realistic result, time and price.
I can keep a client comfortable, private and respected during a service.
I can behave ethically: honest, within my training, safe and confidential.
I can treat every client fairly and adapt for special needs.
I can work as part of a team, and help my internal customers.
I can handle a complaint step by step, know when to call the supervisor and record it.
I can collect feedback, work out average scores, draw a bar chart and plan improvements.
I can build loyalty with records, aftercare advice, rebooking and follow-up.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give a reason for each step and an example. For example: 'I move the client to a quiet area, so that she can speak freely and other clients are not upset.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Client (customer) service
Everything a salon does to meet clients' needs and make them feel valued.
External customer
A person from outside the business who buys its services.
Internal customer
A co-worker who depends on you to do her own job.
Walk-in
A client who comes in without an appointment.
First impression
The opinion a client forms in the first few seconds of meeting you.
Service standards
The salon's own rules for how every client is looked after.
Word of mouth
Free advertising when clients tell others about the salon.
Tone of voice
How your voice sounds, which shows your feelings.
Body language
Your face, eyes, posture and gestures.
Active listening
Giving full attention and checking that you understand.
Open question
A question that needs more than yes or no.
Closed question
A question that can be answered with yes or no.
Rapport
A friendly, trusting relationship with the client.
Empathy
Understanding and sharing how another person feels.
Consultation
A private talk before the service to agree the plan.
Contra-indication
A reason not to give a service, or to change it.
Skin (patch) test
A small test on the skin before a product is used, to check for an allergy.
Ethics
Standards of right and wrong behaviour that guide a professional.
Confidentiality
Keeping a client's personal details private.
Discrimination
Treating a person unfairly because of who she is.
Punctual
Always on time for work and appointments.
Service recovery
Putting things right and winning back a client after a mistake.
Supervisor
The senior person who decides on matters beyond your authority.
Complaint record
A written account of a complaint, the solution and the follow-up.
Client satisfaction
How pleased a client is that the service met her needs.
Average (mean)
The total of the scores divided by the number of scores.
Loyalty card
A card stamped at each visit that gives a reward after a set number of visits.
Aftercare
Advice on caring for the result at home.
Going the extra mile
A small extra act of care beyond what was asked.

c1.title: A busy Saturday in Half-Way Tree
c1.text: It is 11:20 a.m. on a Saturday at a salon in Half-Way Tree, Kingston. All four stylists are busy and the next free chair is in about 50 minutes. Trainee Shevon is on the reception desk. A client booked for 11:00, Kadian, has been waiting 20 minutes, is sighing and keeps checking her watch. Then Mrs. Icilda Grant, aged 67, walks in without a booking and asks for a wash and set. She is hard of hearing and the music and dryers are loud.

c2.title: Sore scalp after braids in Portmore
c2.text: Three days ago trainee Yolanda put box braids on Ms. Tamika Francis in a Portmore salon. At 4 p.m. on a busy afternoon Tamika walks in and says loudly, in front of other clients, that her scalp is sore, she has headaches and 'you ruined my head'. She wants her money back. The supervisor, Mr. Dwayne Lyn, is in the back room.

c3.title: A guest at an Ocho Rios hotel spa
c3.text: Mr. Alan Whitfield, a hotel guest from England who uses a wheelchair, has booked a back massage at a spa in Ocho Rios. The treatment room has a small step at the door. During the massage, with Mr. Whitfield covered by a towel, the therapist's co-worker Kemar opens the door without knocking to ask to borrow some oil. Later, in the staff room, Kemar tells other staff about a large scar he noticed on Mr. Whitfield's back.

c4.title: Feedback cards at the Centre's training salon
c4.text: In the Centre's training salon in Mandeville, five clients filled in an anonymous feedback card and scored each question from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent). Welcome: 5, 5, 4, 5, 5. Waiting time: 3, 2, 3, 4, 3. Cleanliness: 5, 4, 5, 5, 4. Advice on aftercare: 4, 4, 3, 4, 4. Two comments said, 'Lovely staff, but we waited too long.'

c5.title: Products, photos and cover in Spanish Town
c5.text: Trainee Renae works in a salon in Spanish Town where staff earn a small commission on products sold. Her client Lisa has dry, relaxed hair. The salon's dearest conditioner is made for oily hair; a cheaper one on the shelf suits dry hair well. When the style is finished, Renae wants to post a photo of Lisa's face on the salon's Instagram page. Meanwhile stylist Dian gets an urgent call about a family emergency and must leave, with her client half-way through a treatment.

c6.title: Late arrivals in Savanna-la-Mar
c6.text: Ms. Beverley Chin owns a small salon in Savanna-la-Mar. Many clients arrive late or do not turn up, so she wants a written policy. One morning Mr. Hopeton Lewis arrives 25 minutes late for a one-hour haircut booking. The stylist has another booking straight afterwards.

questions.q: What should Shevon do about Mrs. Grant, the walk-in?
o: Tell her the wait is about 50 minutes, offer a seat and a drink, and let her choose
Say a chair will be free 'in a few minutes' so that she stays and does not go to another salon
Say the salon is full today and that walk-ins are not accepted on Saturdays, so she must book
Ask a stylist to hurry the booked client so that Mrs. Grant can be seen at once
questions.why: A walk-in should be told the truth about the wait and given the choice. A false promise leads to a complaint, and pushing a booked client aside is unfair to her.

questions.q: Kadian has waited 20 minutes and keeps sighing and looking at her watch. What is the best response?
o: Go to her, apologise, say how long it will be and offer a drink
Say that all clients wait on Saturdays, so she should be patient
Leave her alone, as she has a booking and must expect to wait
Tell her that the stylist will rush her service to save time
questions.why: Her body language shows she is getting unhappy. Apologising, giving a realistic time and offering a drink shows respect. Rushing the service later would lower the quality.

questions.q: Mrs. Grant says she cannot hear well. How should Shevon speak to her?
o: Shout so that she can hear over the noise
Speak quickly and a little louder, so that the visit does not take longer
Face her, speak clearly and slowly, and move to a quieter spot
Speak to her relative, if there is one, and not to her
questions.why: A client who is hard of hearing needs you to face her so she can see your lips, to speak clearly and a little slower (not louder), and to reduce noise. Always speak to the client herself.

questions.q: Tamika is complaining loudly in front of other clients. What should Yolanda do first?
o: Ask her to lower her voice, because other clients can hear
Invite her to a quiet area and listen to the whole complaint
Explain that the braids were done exactly as she asked
Tell her that the supervisor will deal with it tomorrow
questions.why: Moving the client to a quiet area lets her speak freely and calms the situation. Listening without interrupting comes before explaining or defending.

questions.q: After listening, which reply is best?
o: 'Braids always feel tight at first, so it will pass in a day or two.'
'I am sorry your scalp is sore. Let me look at your braids to see what is wrong.'
'You should have told me while I was doing them, and then I would have loosened them.'
'I will give you your money back now so that you can go home.'
questions.why: This apologises for her pain without arguing, and moves to checking the facts. The other replies dismiss her, blame her, or promise a refund the trainee is not allowed to give.

questions.q: Tamika insists on a full refund. What should Yolanda do?
o: Refuse politely, because the braids were done as booked
Offer half the money back to settle the matter quickly
Say she will return, ask her supervisor to decide, and stay with Tamika
Give the refund from the till and tell the supervisor afterwards
questions.why: Refunds and compensation are normally the supervisor's decision. Calling the supervisor, and staying with the client, keeps her from having to wait alone or repeat everything.

questions.q: The supervisor looks at the scalp, agrees to loosen the front braids at no charge and advises Tamika to see a doctor if the soreness continues. Which record is best?
o: The date, the client's name, the amount refunded and the stylist's name
'Client complained about her braids; resolved to her satisfaction on the day'
Her complaint, the findings, the action agreed and by whom, and a follow-up date
A note on the stylist's own file only, so that the client's record stays clean
questions.why: A full record (complaint, findings, agreed action, who agreed and follow-up) lets the manager spot a pattern, such as braids put in too tight, and protects staff and client if the issue returns.

questions.q: Before Mr. Whitfield arrives, what should the spa do about the step at the treatment room door?
o: Plan to carry his chair over the step when he arrives
Ask him to arrange his own helper, since he booked the treatment
Move the massage to a different day when the step is fixed
Ask what help he needs and arrange a ramp or a ground-level room
questions.why: Ask the client what help she or he wants and prepare in advance. Carrying a wheelchair is unsafe and undignified, and a client should not have to bring her own helper to use a service.

questions.q: What should Kemar have done before he came into the treatment room?
o: Walked in quickly, as the client was covered by a towel
Asked another therapist to go in for him and fetch the oil
Waited until the massage ended and gone in without noise
Knocked, waited for a reply and kept the client's privacy
questions.why: A client who is undressed has a right to privacy and dignity. Even when she is covered, staff must knock and wait, and avoid interrupting a treatment unless necessary.

questions.q: A therapist hears Kemar describe Mr. Whitfield's scar to other staff. What should she do?
o: Join in, as the guest is from abroad and will not find out who spoke about it
Remind Kemar politely that client details are private, and tell the supervisor if it goes on
Say nothing, because it is not her client and it is not her business to interfere
Tell the other guests the story first, so that it will not be spread by Kemar
questions.why: What you see or hear about a client's body or health is confidential. Staff should correct each other politely and involve the supervisor if it continues.

questions.q: What is the average score for 'Advice on aftercare'?
questions.why: The scores 4 + 4 + 3 + 4 + 4 total 19. Divide by 5 clients: 19 ÷ 5 = 3.8.

questions.q: Which question should the salon work on first?
o: Waiting time, which has the lowest average (3.0)
Cleanliness, because clients notice it more than anything else
Welcome, because first impressions matter most
Advice on aftercare, because it is the next lowest score
questions.why: Waiting time totals 15, so its average is 3.0, the lowest, and the comments agree. Work first on the lowest scores and on points that clients mention again and again.

questions.q: Which improvement plan for the waiting-time score is best?
o: Remove the waiting-time question from the card, so the scores look better
Ask the staff to try harder to keep to time and not to chat so much with clients
Tell clients to book earlier in the day, to avoid the busiest times on Saturdays
Tell clients the expected wait and offer a drink, from Monday, and check scores in four weeks
questions.why: A good plan says what will change, who will do it and by when, and how it will be checked. 'Try harder' is vague, and hiding the question or blaming clients solves nothing.

questions.q: What should Renae recommend to Lisa?
o: The dearest conditioner, as it is the best-known product
The cheaper conditioner that suits dry hair, and explain why
No conditioner at all, to avoid over-selling her anything
Whichever product earns the salon the most commission
questions.why: Honest selling means recommending what suits the client and explaining why, even when it earns less. Pushing a product that does not suit her damages trust and the result.

questions.q: Renae wants to post Lisa's finished style on Instagram. What should she do?
o: Post only the back of the hair and the name of the salon, without asking
Post it at once, because the style is the salon's work
Ask for Lisa's permission first, and note it on her record, and respect a 'no'
Post a picture of the face only if the client smiled in the mirror
questions.why: A client's picture is her personal information. She must agree first, and the agreement should be recorded. Some clients prefer not to be photographed at all.

questions.q: Dian must leave in the middle of her client's treatment. What is the best way to handle it?
o: Leave quickly and trust that the client will not notice the change at all
Ask the client to come back another day and stop the treatment halfway through
Ask Renae to finish the treatment, without telling the client why it has changed
Agree a hand-over with the supervisor and tell the client what has changed
questions.why: A smooth hand-over agreed by the supervisor, with the client told and clear information passed on, keeps the service safe and professional. Leaving a treatment unfinished or switching stylists in silence upsets clients.

questions.q: How should the stylist treat Mr. Lewis, who is 25 minutes late?
o: Refuse to serve him and tell him to book again, so that others will learn to be on time
Do the full haircut anyway, even though the next client will have to wait much longer
Scold him in front of the other clients, so that he never comes late again
Greet him politely, explain what fits in the time left, and offer a shorter cut or a new time
questions.why: Stay polite, be honest about what is possible in the time left and offer options. This respects the next client too. Scolding or sending him away damages the relationship, and overrunning is unfair to the next client.

questions.q: Which late-arrival policy would be fair?
o: Written, explained at booking and applied to all, with the supervisor deciding on emergencies
Applied only to clients the owner does not know well, and not to her friends or family
Kept unwritten, so that the owner can decide on the day what to do with each client
Explained to each client only after she has already arrived late for her booking
questions.why: A fair policy is written, explained in advance and applied equally, with room for real emergencies. Applying it differently to different clients is discrimination, and a surprise rule is likely to cause complaints.

questions.q: A receptionist answers the salon phone. Which is the best start to the call?
o: 'Yes?' in a quiet voice, so that other clients are not disturbed
'Hello, who is this?', so that she can decide how to answer
'Good morning, Bloom Salon, this is Marcia. How may I help you?'
'Hold on', followed by a pause while she finishes what she was doing
questions.why: A good phone greeting gives a greeting, the salon's name and your own name, in a warm voice, and invites the caller to say what she needs.

questions.q: A client says she is nervous about her first eyebrow wax. Which reply shows empathy?
o: 'Don't worry, it is nothing. Everyone gets waxed and nobody makes a fuss about it.'
'It is normal to feel nervous. I will tell you each step, and you can ask me to stop.'
'You should have thought about that before you booked.'
'It will hurt a little, but you will get used to it, so try to relax and keep still.'
questions.why: Empathy means understanding how she feels and responding to it. The best reply accepts her feeling, explains what will happen and gives her control. The other replies dismiss or ignore her feelings.
